prompt.brief: Design a fair, abuse-resistant flash-distribution system that gives away six million vouchers or burgers in one hour while keeping inventory, eligibility, and redemption correct under extreme concurrency.
successSignals: Define eligibility, fairness, admission, reservation, redemption, expiry, and inventory ledgers with an idempotency key per user/campaign.
Absorb millions of arrivals with waiting-room admission, bot defenses, quotas, randomized or timestamped ordering, and bounded queues.
Keep the hot path small and asynchronous; make inventory allocation atomic and reconcile abandoned reservations and store redemptions durably.
Explain regional capacity, retries, fraud, queue failure, campaign pause/resume, observability, and a transparent sold-out mode.

functional: Admit eligible users, issue a fair position/token, reserve an item, confirm redemption, and expose queue and reservation status.
Enforce one-per-user/device limits, campaign windows, inventory variants, expiration, cancellation, and store/fulfillment handoff.
Make retries safe, prevent oversell and double redemption, audit decisions, and recover from queue, payment-free fulfillment, or region failures.
nonFunctional: Absorb at least 10 million arrival attempts in an hour while keeping allocation correctness and a bounded admission response.
Distribute six million successful allocations without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 10M arrivals/hour and 6M available items across thousands of stores
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

dataFlow.title: Search and price current candidates
dataFlow.description: The backend query path combines catalog, eligibility, price, and current availability without treating a stale index as a final claim.

dataFlow.title: Claim scarce inventory
dataFlow.description: The backend service creates a short-lived conditional claim keyed by item and request idempotency before charging or confirming.

architecture.title: Backend domain architecture
architecture.summary: Design a fair, abuse-resistant flash-distribution system that gives away six million vouchers or burgers in one hour while keeping inventory, eligibility, and redemption correct under extreme concurrency. The design makes backend decisions durable, isolates slow or external work behind replayable boundaries, and exposes freshness, authorization, and recovery state to operators and clients.

layers.label: Booking reliability operations

deepDives.title: Inventory claims and oversell control
points: Use conditional writes or a serialized inventory partition for backend scarce capacity.
Give holds an expiry and reaper, but never release a confirmed claim from a stale worker.
Separate searchable availability from the authoritative claim path.

deepDives.title: Payment and unknown outcomes
points: Bind backend payment attempts to the intent and request hash, not just the customer session.
Treat timeout as unknown, query or reconcile provider state, and avoid a blind second charge.
Keep sensitive payment tokens outside business records and logs.

deepDives.title: Fulfillment and partner recovery
points: Publish backend events after commit, consume at least once, and track per-stage progress.
Use reconciliation against partner feeds or delivery evidence instead of assuming a callback arrives.
Expose pending and expired status so the client can explain what happened.

tradeoffs.title: Reservation versus oversell tolerance
tradeoffs.recommendation: Prefer a short-lived backend claim for scarce inventory and state the consistency scope explicitly.
tradeoffs.caution: A cache or search index cannot safely decrement the final room count.

tradeoffs.title: Synchronous checkout versus asynchronous fulfillment
tradeoffs.recommendation: Commit the reservation intent synchronously and move partner or delivery work behind events.
tradeoffs.caution: Waiting for downstream fulfillment makes retries ambiguous and increases checkout tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Precompute availability versus compute at read time
tradeoffs.recommendation: Precompute common search dimensions but validate the final claim against authoritative state.
tradeoffs.caution: Serving only a precomputed backend availability view creates oversell or stale-price failures.

commonMistakes: Charging before a backend inventory claim is durable.
Retrying a timed-out payment without resolving the first attempt.
Letting stale search results act as the final availability decision.
Making cancellation and hold expiry non-idempotent.
Failing to reconcile late partner confirmations, refunds, or delivery failures.

followUps.question: How do you avoid double reservations?
followUps.answer: Persist the backend request idempotency key, condition the intent transition, and make inventory, payment, and fulfillment consumers deduplicate the same command.

followUps.question: What if inventory changes between search and checkout?
followUps.answer: Recheck authoritative availability, return an explicit unavailable or repriced result, and do not silently convert a failed claim into a confirmed one.

followUps.question: How do you repair a stuck fulfillment?
followUps.answer: Use an operation timeline, provider evidence, retry-safe transitions, and an operator-approved compensating action or cancellation.

rubric.description: The answer addresses the backend workflow, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure contract.
The answer identifies the authoritative backend state, versioning or deduplication boundary, and how derived views converge.
The answer partitions backend traffic, isolates hot keys, and moves fan-out, retries, or rebuilds behind bounded asynchronous work.
The answer names freshness, backlog, error, cost, and recovery signals tied to the backend user experience.
